British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
<scp>GenAI</scp>
                    ‐based metacognitive prompting in collaborative inquiry: A comparison across diverse preconception groups
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into collaborative inquiry to provide metacognitive prompting that scaffolds socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL). Understanding how such GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting is taken up through student–GenAI interactions is therefore critical. However, although learner–GenAI interaction processes have been widely examined, little is known about how learners' preconceptions shape their engagement with GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting. This study examined how groups with different or similar preconceptions about energy forms and conservation differed in their engagement with GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting during collaborative inquiry. Participants comprised 14 small groups, including eight groups with different preconceptions (D groups) and six groups with similar preconceptions (S groups). The distribution of learner‐generated inquiries directed to the written metacognitive AI (MAI) was largely comparable across groups. Lag sequential analysis revealed contrasting patterns in how groups evaluated the metacognitive prompts: D groups showed sustained positive or neutral evaluation of the prompts, whereas S groups showed sustained negative evaluation. Process mining further showed that AI query negotiation served as a hub in D groups' collaboration, connecting their conceptual discussions and task coordination. In S groups, by contrast, it formed part of a simpler, linear sequence of querying the AI and processing its responses. This study advances understanding of how preconception diversity shapes the processes and dynamics of human–AI collaboration. The findings show that AI‐mediated regulation varies depending on group‐level knowledge configurations.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic
                          
                            
                              Effective collaborative inquiry depends on learners' prior knowledge resources and their regulatory capacity.
                            
                            
                              Preconceptions, as a core component of prior knowledge, shape how learners interpret problems and engage in conceptual discussion.
                            
                            
                              GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting is designed to externalise metacognitive awareness and scaffold learners' regulatory processes.
                            
                            
                              Regulation unfolds through temporally ordered interaction sequences that reveal underlying regulatory dynamics.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds
                          
                            
                              This study compares how different preconception groups and similar preconception groups engage with GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting during collaborative scientific inquiry.
                            
                            
                              GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting responded to similar types of learner inquiries across groups.
                            
                            
                              GenAI query interaction in different preconception groups appeared more integrated with conceptual and task discussion, whereas in similar preconception groups it followed a more linear, output‐focused path.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and/or policy
                          
                            
                              GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting may benefit from incorporating a preliminary classification layer that distinguishes between metacognitive prompts and procedural or informational requests.
                            
                            
                              Teachers may consider preconception diversity when forming groups, as different epistemic configurations appear to give rise to distinct patterns of GenAI‐learner collaboration.
                            
                            
                              Policymakers and designers should recognise that GenAI functions as a co‐regulator within collaborative settings, and its impact depends on how it is interactionally integrated into group interactional trajectories.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
Generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    as a team moderator in
                    <scp>CSCL</scp>
                    : Facilitating students' multidimensional engagement through adaptive scaffolding for socially shared regulation of learning
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is essential for successful collaboration, yet effectively scaffolding it remains challenging because regulatory needs are dynamic and context‐dependent. While generative AI (GenAI) offers potential for adaptive support, current applications in collaborative learning largely position it as a content‐oriented tutor for knowledge explanation or idea generation, leaving its role as a process‐oriented team moderator for scaffolding SSRL processes underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a 16‐week quasi‐experiment with 64 undergraduates in China, comparing adaptive SSRL scaffolding delivered by a GenAI agent in the adaptive‐SSRL condition with static scaffolding via structured digital worksheets in the static‐SSRL condition. Survey data and group discussion transcripts were analysed using statistical methods and epistemic network analysis. Results indicated several differences in students' multidimensional engagement between the two conditions: (1) Behaviourally, the adaptive‐SSRL group showed significantly higher participation equality, although participation intensity did not differ significantly between groups. (2) Cognitively, the adaptive‐SSRL group demonstrated deeper cognitive engagement, reflected in more advanced cognitive presence phases and more integrative, solution‐oriented discourse patterns. (3) Emotionally, the adaptive‐SSRL group reported significantly higher overall emotional engagement, particularly feeling more relaxed during collaboration and more connected with peers. These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by showing that GenAI can function as an SSRL‐informed team moderator rather than a content‐oriented tutor. They also offer design implications for GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding and human–AI role division in CSCL.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic
                          
                            
                              Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is critical for successful collaboration and is closely associated with the quality of student engagement.
                            
                            
                              While static scaffolds (eg, worksheets) provide a basic regulatory structure, they fail to adapt to the dynamic and emergent needs of collaborating teams.
                            
                            
                              Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used for personalised content support, yet its potential as a process‐oriented team moderator remains underexplored.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds
                          
                            
                              This study introduced SSRLAgent, a GenAI agent grounded in SSRL theory and established principles of collective metacognitive support, to provide adaptive and interactive regulatory scaffolding.
                            
                            
                              In a 16‐week quasi‐experiment, we compared GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding (SSRLAgent) with static scaffolding (structured digital worksheets) in CSCL.
                            
                            
                              Adaptive‐SSRL scaffolding was associated with higher‐quality engagement: greater participation equality, deeper cognitive engagement and higher overall emotional engagement.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and/or policy
                          
                            
                              The study underscores the necessity of shifting SSRL scaffolding from static, ‘one‐size‐fits‐all’ support to adaptive GenAI interventions to improve collaborative engagement.
                            
                            
                              The findings provide design guidance for developing SSRL agents that are embedded in the shared interaction space and responsive to groups' moment‐to‐moment regulatory needs.
                            
                            
                              The study suggests a productive human–AI division of labour: GenAI agents can support process coordination and regulatory prompting, while teachers and peers remain essential for relationally complex forms of support that collaborative learning requires.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation.
                  
                    
                      
                        Practitioner notes
                      
                      
                        What is already known about this topic
                        
                          
                            Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking.
                          
                          
                            Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes.
                          
                          
                            Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions.
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        What this paper adds
                        
                          
                            An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting.
                          
                          
                            Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT.
                          
                          
                            Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity.
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        Implications for practice and/or policy
                        
                          
                            Prompt engineering can be used to simulate emotional support and personalize guidance based on SRL and emotion regulation principles, providing design considerations for future learner‐centred GenAI systems.
                          
                          
                            Developers and educators aiming to design pedagogically meaningful GenAI tools should focus on scaffolding SRL both cognitively and emotionally, to support the affective and self‐regulatory dimensions of learning.
                          
                          
                            We make the technical specifications and system prompts publicly available.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Should there be a teacher in-the-loop? A study of generative AI-personalized tasks middle school
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  Large language models can be used to design instructional tasks to align to students’ needs. These generative AI models can create tasks that correspond to students’ out-of-school interests in areas like sports or music, which may enhance students’ interest in learning. However, little is known about teachers’ processes for creating or modifying tasks with generative AI, despite commercial AI companies’ claims that they will save teachers time. In the present study, 7 middle school mathematics teachers used ChatGPT to create personalized versions of problems in their curriculum to correspond to their students’ interests. The prompting moves teachers made and their students’ open-ended feedback on personalized problems were examined through thematic analysis. Teachers’ efficiency when creating problems and the ratings of their 7th grade students who received personalized assignments were examined. Results from this sample suggest that having a teacher-in-the-loop may result in generative AI-enhanced personalization being enacted at a broad grain size, whereas students often expressed preference for a smaller grain-size where they receive specific popular culture references that interest them. Teachers used prompting to adjust popular culture references and address issues with the depth, ethics, or realism of the problems generated, in some cases showing epistemic agency. The article closes with an exploratory, design-focused look at scalability trade-offs with teacher-facing personalization, patterns of teacher prompting practices, and opportunities for teachers to exercise epistemic and ethical monitoring of personalization outputs.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Artificial intelligence and empathetic communication to enhance learning engagement, motivation, and effectiveness
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  With advances in artificial intelligence (AI), textual sentiment analysis has become increasingly popular for extracting word relationships and uncovering hidden emotions. This study applied sentiment analysis to explore students’ emotions during learning because emotions significantly impact motivation and outcomes. Effective teacher-student communication fosters understanding and enhances learning but requires strong empathetic skills to recognize and address students’ emotions. To support this, we developed an AI-assisted learning system integrating KeyMoji, ChatGPT, and Unity that analyzes emotions in real time and provides empathetic responses. The results showed that learning emotions were associated with teacher-student interactions and self-reported academic performance. Students who reported receiving empathetic responses also reported higher engagement and perceived learning outcomes, although these relationships cannot be interpreted as causal given the study design. This study provides preliminary evidence that AI sentiment analysis and empathetic communication are statistically associated with students’ learning emotions, motivation, engagement, and perceived learning outcomes. These findings suggest that AI-generated empathetic feedback supports effective motivational learning processes. The post-test findings indicate that AI-generated empathetic feedback is statistically associated with perceived learning outcomes indirectly through learning emotions and motivation, although these relationships should be interpreted as associational rather than causal, given the post-test single-group research design. Consequently, this study provides a transferable blueprint that advances both affective computing theory and practical digital pedagogy.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
Designing Teaching Agents for Human‐
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    Collaborative Classrooms: A Design‐Based Study of Students' Sense of Presence and Learning Engagement
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Generative artificial intelligence has expanded the possibilities for teaching agents to provide instructional explanations and feedback. However, limited research has examined how such support can be integrated into teacher‐guided classroom instruction and how students experience and engage with this form of teaching.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study aimed to iteratively design and refine teaching agents within a teacher‐guided undergraduate classroom and to examine changes in students' sense of presence and learning engagement across three design iterations.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    A single‐group design‐based research study was conducted in a 10‐week Introduction to Educational Technology course. 36 first‐year undergraduate students majoring in educational technology participated in three design iterations: gesture‐supported presentation, teacher‐mediated real‐time Q&A, and individualized text‐based Q&A. Data were collected through questionnaires, classroom observations, student feedback, question records, and discussion texts. Repeated‐measures analyses were used to examine changes in students' sense of presence and learning engagement, and epistemic network analysis was used to examine changes in co‐occurrence patterns among presence‐related codes in students' post‐class reflections.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    The findings show that students' sense of presence significantly increased across the three iterations, whereas learning engagement did not show a statistically significant change, although the descriptive means showed a small upward pattern. Epistemic network analysis identified changes in co‐occurrence patterns among presence‐related codes in students' post‐class reflections. The strongest connections involved direct instruction, affective expression, and resolution in the first iteration, and affective expression with direct instruction, exploration, and integration in the third iteration. Given the single‐group sequential design, these findings should be interpreted as observed changes during the iterative implementation process rather than causal evidence for the independent effects of specific design strategies. The study contributes process‐oriented evidence and design considerations for integrating teaching agents into teacher‐orchestrated human‐AI collaborative classrooms.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
<scp>ChatGPT</scp>
                    ‐Supported Literary Translation: Tense Accuracy and Dynamic Emotion Profiles in the Language Classroom
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Generative artificial intelligence can facilitate task completion, but whether it improves learning or consistently shapes task‐related emotions remains unclear.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This mixed‐methods classroom study compared literary translation with ChatGPT access, translation with dictionary access and optional teacher assistance and regular instruction, focusing on tense accuracy and task‐related emotional experiences.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    The study involved 42 English‐major undergraduates. All participants completed a pretest and a posttest of English tense use. The 29 students in the translation conditions completed six translation tasks and provided 556 repeated emotion‐bar records with concurrent written explanations; 10 of these students also participated in interviews. Robust analysis of covariance, within‐participant models, exploratory configurational measures and thematic analysis were used.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    Mean scores increased in all three conditions, but adjusted posttest scores and gain scores did not differ significantly among them. No statistically significant between‐condition differences were detected in individual‐emotion percentages or configurational measures. None of the six emotion percentages varied significantly across task sessions, although curiosity was lower at the fourth than at the first measurement point. Profile mixedness was lower in Task 5 (Session 6) than in Task 2 (Session 3). Qualitative findings linked emotions mainly to text content and difficulty, progress, time pressure and classroom conditions. ChatGPT was valued for its speed and immediacy but raised concerns about reliability, effort and ownership.
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    The study did not detect a statistically significant advantage for ChatGPT support in tense accuracy or emotional experience. The exploratory configurational analysis nevertheless identified a task‐session difference not apparent in the separate emotion percentages, illustrating the value of examining learning outcomes, repeated emotion reports and students' appraisals together when evaluating AI‐supported language tasks.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: From Design to Classroom Adoption: Teachers' Perspectives on AI‐powered Writing Analytics in Resource‐Constrained Contexts
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    The adoption of automated tools to support teaching and learning processes has been widely discussed in the literature. However, there remains a need for user‐oriented designs that better align with teachers' practices and classroom realities while providing actionable insights to support instructional choices in authentic educational settings.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study aims to systematically evaluate the usability, acceptability and pedagogical relevance of an AIED‐Unplugged learning analytics tool from teachers' perspectives, in order to guide the development of user‐centered design strategies and support writing practices in resource‐constrained educational settings without deepening digital inequities. The proposed study also aims to derive pedagogical and user‐centered design recommendations to strengthen the development of AIED‐U solutions for resource‐constrained educational settings.
                  
                  
                    Method
                    We employed a mixed‐methods approach involving nine teachers, who downloaded an AIED‐U application and followed a predefined usage scenario according to a think‐aloud protocol. Afterwards, participants filled out the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and System Usability Scale (SUS) questionnaires, taking part in a moderated semi‐structured interview guided by an interview script.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusion
                    The study shows how AI‐driven educational tools can support personalization and the development of essay‐writing activities in resource‐constrained contexts while optimizing teachers'time and contributing to students' writing development. The quantitative findings indicated high levels of acceptance and usability, corroborating the qualitative findings that teachers perceived the solution as useful, easy to integrate and supportive of their practices. Taken together, these findings provide empirical evidence of teachers' perceptions regarding the tool's usability, usefulness and potential applicability within authentic classroom workflows in resource‐constrained educational environments.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
Beyond Access: How
                    <scp>GenAI</scp>
                    Literacy Relates to Task Performance, Motivation, Cognitive Load and Interaction Patterns in
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    ‐Assisted Learning Environment
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Generative AI is rapidly being integrated into educational settings, yet equitable benefits depend heavily on students' GenAI literacy. While access to these tools is increasing, empirical evidence remains limited on how specific dimensions of assessed GenAI literacy relate to students' task performance, cognitive experiences, and actual interactional behaviours during learning.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study examined the associations of overall GenAI literacy and its four dimensions (Know and Understand, Use and Apply, Evaluate and Create, Ethics) with students' abstract‐writing performance, self‐efficacy, motivation, and cognitive load. It also explored how assessed literacy is reflected in the configurations of students' interactions with GenAI.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    A total of 162 university students completed an abstract‐writing task using a custom GenAI assistant. Ordinary least‐squares regression models evaluated the continuous GenAI literacy scores against writing performance, motivation, and cognitive load, adjusting for prior academic writing knowledge and English proficiency. Additionally, Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) was applied to conversational trace data to compare the configurations of questioning and commanding behaviours between higher‐ and lower‐literacy students.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    Higher overall GenAI literacy was positively associated with better writing performance and negatively associated with perceived mental load. Dimension‐level analyses revealed distinct roles: the Use and Apply dimension was independently associated with higher writing performance, while the Know and Understand dimension was uniquely associated with lower mental load. Neither the total score nor the sub‐dimensions showed reliable associations with motivation or self‐efficacy. Furthermore, ENA profiles demonstrated that higher‐literacy students engaged in a refinement‐oriented process, whereas lower‐literacy students relied predominantly on direct content generation and factual retrieval. These findings suggest that instruction should address both conceptual understanding and practical application of GenAI, helping students critically evaluate and refine AI‐generated content during writing.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Unraveling the Effects of Block-Based Visual Programming on Students’ Computational Thinking
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Nowadays, computational thinking has been the core necessary skill for students who want to succeed in the 21
                    st
                    century. Block-based visual programming (BBVP) is one of the most widely used ways to develop student computational thinking. However, its impact on student computational thinking is mixed in the education field. This study conducts a meta-analysis to compare the impacts of BBVP and textual programming on student computational thinking. The result covering 24 independent studies and 2,441 students indicates that BBVP has a large positive effect (
                    SMD
                    = 0.887,
                    CI
                    = [0.625, 1.148],
                    p
                    < 0.001) on student computational thinking. We also conduct moderator analysis and find that class size, treatment duration, test type, BBVP type, subject, learning method, and region significantly moderate BBVP’s impacts on students computational thinking. Finally, major findings, recommendations, and limitations are provided.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Toward an Interpretive Synthesis of Personalization, Co-Design, and Ethical Mediation in AI-Supported Higher Education: An Integrative Review of Agentic, Generative, and Adaptive Tutoring Systems
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies are expanding in higher education, raising questions about their alignment with pedagogical goals. This qualitative-integrative review synthesizes 57 publications (21 empirical, 25 conceptual or framework, 9 systematic reviews or meta-analyses retained for triangulation, and 2 design/development papers) from 2024 to 2026, employing Whittemore and Knafl’s methodology to examine AI-supported tutoring, implementation strategies, and learner/instructor experiences. Three interpretive themes organize this heterogeneous evidence: (1) personalization as a recurring target, from micro-level adaptation to curriculum design; (2) technology-pedagogy co-design as a recurring implementation pattern; and (3) contextual and ethical conditions surrounding adoption, including culture, policy gaps, well-being, and academic integrity. These themes are interpretive, not a validated framework, and draw on evidence of uneven strength. The present review does not estimate effect sizes or pool outcomes across studies; g = 0.70, reported by X. Wang et al. in a separate meta-analysis of 45 studies (2010–2022) of pre-generative adaptive systems, which is cited only as background, not as a finding of this review. Implications are framed as evidence-tiered hypotheses, while the layered model is offered as an interpretive scaffold for future research, not a confirmatory model.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: How Generative AI-Assisted Formative Feedback Is Appraised and Implemented in Online Collaborative Learning
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Effective educational feedback is vital for enhancing student learning, yet providing personalized formative feedback in large-class settings remains challenging. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) offers a potential means of scaling formative feedback. Guided by a self-determination theory-based model, this study examines the features, implementation, and pre-service teachers’ perceptions of generative AI-assisted formative feedback (GAI-FF) at a university in China. Participants (
                    n
                    = 114) received four types of GAI-FF, varying in complexity and focus, across three feedback intervals during a semester. Feedback content and written reflections were analyzed using content analysis, epistemic network analysis, and thematic analysis. Results indicate that (1) GAI can generate formative feedback with distinct cognitive and affective feature patterns; (2) overall implementation of GAI-FF was limited; (3) feedback containing problem identification, suggestions, and solutions was more likely to be enacted, whereas feedback emphasizing affective features was less frequently implemented; and (4) participants expressed mixed perceptions, recognizing the usefulness of GAI-FF for collaborative learning while also noting constraints related to rigidity, accuracy, and practical applicability. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of GAI-FF depends on how it supports learners’ cognitive, motivational, and affective appraisals, which shape subsequent feedback use. The study also highlights the importance of deliberate instructional design and cautious integration of GAI tools in formative assessment practices.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Socratic, Artifact-Gated Generative AI Scaffolding in a 6E Inquiry Unit: A Clustered Quasi-Experiment in Elementary Students’ Computational Thinking
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Open-ended computational thinking (CT) inquiry challenges one teacher to support learners progressing at different rates. This clustered quasi-experiment evaluated TALPer, a generative-AI tutor providing student-initiated, artifact-contingent Socratic prompts during a six-lesson 6E unit. Ten intact Grade 3 classes in Taiwan (N = 229) completed the same curriculum, tasks, teacher, platform, and instructional time. Conditions differed in a bundled scaffolding configuration involving source, delivery modality, initiation, privacy, and artifact requirements. A two-level model controlling for pretest CT estimated an adjusted posttest difference favoring TALPer (
                    B
                    = 4.05,
                    SE

                    p
                    = .011; sensitivity
                    p
                    = .034; Hedges’
                    g

Findings provide preliminary evidence concerning the bundled intervention but do not isolate component contributions.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: From Prompting to Scaffolding: Divergent Human–AI Interaction Pathways of Pre-Service Teachers in Multi-Agent Micro-Teaching Simulation (MAMS)
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Traditional micro-teaching offers limited opportunities for pre-service teachers to rehearse classroom contingencies in repeatable, standardized ways. This study developed a multi-agent micro-teaching simulation (MAMS), informed by professional noticing, to expand practice-based learning opportunities for pre-service mathematics teachers (PSTs). MAMS integrates differentiated virtual students, standardized challenge events, and Dean Agent prompts to create comparable classroom contingencies. Sixty-four PSTs completed two simulated micro-teaching sessions and were analytically classified into higher and lower baseline mathematics pedagogical content knowledge (MPCK) profiles. Outcomes included teacher self-efficacy, MPCK performance, and Community of Inquiry presence; interaction logs were analyzed using event-anchored lag sequential analysis. Under the standardized MAMS condition, outcome analyses showed observed pre–post changes and modest baseline-adjusted profile differences. The higher baseline MPCK profile showed stronger MPCK response-strategy performance and higher Teaching Presence; Social and Cognitive Presence showed no reliable profile differences. Log analyses revealed divergent feedback-to-action pathways: higher baseline MPCK PSTs more often moved from Dean Agent prompts to diagnostic questioning and scaffolding, followed by substantive student responses, whereas lower baseline MPCK PSTs more often shifted to direct instruction or process regulation, followed by continued low participation. These findings suggest a need for prior-knowledge-responsive scaffolding in AI-supported teacher education.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: What counts as digital play? Irish early childhood educators’ beliefs and practice tensions
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Digital technologies are increasingly embedded in young children’s lives, yet uncertainty remains regarding their role in early childhood education and care (ECEC). This study explores Irish early years educators’ beliefs and perceptions concerning digital play, employing Bronfenbrenner’s bioecological framework to examine how policy, parental expectations and professional identity interact to shape children’s learning opportunities. Semi-structured interviews with 10 educators identified five themes: developmentalist beliefs prioritising ‘natural’ play, cautious openness to digital tools, professional identity and ethical tensions, perceptions of children and families and concerns about policy directives. Findings reveal a persistent policy–practice gap, where limited professional development and unclear guidance leave educators uncertain about how to define and implement quality digital play. The study emphasises that educators’ attitudes are closely associated with the extent and quality of children’s digital engagement, highlighting the need for sustained professional development and strengthened mesosystemic communication across home, school and policy contexts. Implications include the creation of context-sensitive frameworks that integrate digital and traditional play while supporting children’s holistic development. This study demonstrates that educators’ definitions of digital play are shaped by the interaction of professional identity, policy ambiguity, family expectations and resource conditions, offering new insight into the conditions that constrain digital play in Irish early years settings.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Teachers’ professional learning and development experiences in Chinese kindergartens: Opportunities and tensions
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Professional learning and development (PLD) activities for Chinese kindergarten teachers have introduced imported knowledge to promote teaching and learning. Much PLD provision is led by leaders and experts rather than teachers. To understand the educational beliefs and power differences that surface among teachers, leaders and experts during PLD sessions and how teachers navigate this complex terrain, this paper presents a post-intentional phenomenological study involving seven participants from two Chinese early childhood settings. Data collection included semi-structured interviews, observations of PLD meetings and videos of teachers’ implementation of PLD ideas. Educational policies, PLD materials, and the researcher’s reflexive journal were also used for analysis. Analysis involved a line-by-line reading process where theoretical concepts, data and researcher reflexivity interacted. The findings reveal that teachers experienced tensions in relation to formal PLD sessions. These tensions stemmed from established values and hierarchical constraints that limited their joint reflection and actions. Our analysis, framed by the concepts of relational agency and in-between spaces, shows how teachers navigated these tensions. Despite these constraints, the teachers responded by creating opportunities for collaborative learning. They sought out informal situations where they had the flexibility to develop shared knowledge. We argue that Chinese teachers’ PLD can occur within and across such tensions and opportunities. These informal situations empowered teachers to enact relational agency by aligning their expertise to make PLD decisions. This process eased tensions and created space for collaborative learning. The study concludes that valuing these informal, teacher-initiated spaces is crucial for moving beyond top-down knowledge transmission and fostering sustainable professional growth in hierarchical educational contexts. Ultimately, by empowering teachers as collaborative and adaptable professionals, this model of PLD offers new insights into enhancing the professional environments that shape teaching practice and young children’s learning.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Parent–school mobile communication in preschool: A qualitative study in Mexico
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: School-family communication in early childhood is increasingly mediated by mobile applications, yet important questions remain about what counts as high-quality content, how schools allocate topics between digital and face-to-face channels, and what costs these practices impose on teachers. This qualitative study examines how a mobile application shapes day-to-day parent-school communication in a Mexican preschool. Semi-structured interviews with four teachers and three mothers, combined with field observation, were thematically analyzed. The app supported timely and consistent exchanges about classroom life. Families valued brief, concrete descriptions of children’s socio-emotional participation, peer interactions, and strategies practiced, along with simple suggestions for follow-up at home. However, participants identified a depth gap when messages focused mainly on logistics, and teachers reported a workload tension between the burden of exhaustive daily reporting and the sense of security it provides to parents. A hybrid model of communication was preferred: routine updates and nonurgent questions were handled in the app, while complex, evaluative, or sensitive topics were addressed in planned one-to-one meetings. Reported short-term gains were primarily psychosocial, including higher trust and a closer working relationship between teachers and families. Findings support a shift from tool adoption to the quality of communicative practice in early childhood settings.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Promoting social skills and friendships in early childhood education: A case study of four children’s trajectories to inclusion
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: This paper reports on the changes reported on the social relations and skills of four children after the implementation of ProFriend (Promoting Friendship) in an early childhood education (ECE) setting. ProFriend is a programme developed considering the inclusive ECE principles by targeting all children’s access and participation and looking beyond imposed labels. The data of the study included friendship nominations, observations, children’s drawings, teachers’ interviews and research diary. The findings shed light on four children’s trajectories who faced challenges in forming friendships and whose individual characteristics (speech and language impairments and socio-emotional difficulties) were seen by teachers as barriers to their social development. The discussion focuses on how children’s exclusion can be minimised by enriching ECE curricula with some elements guiding teachers on how to approach the development of social skills and friendships in a meaningful and inclusive way.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: The impact of active transitions on preschool students’ self-regulation
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Early childhood education plays a pivotal role in fostering the holistic development of young learners through age-appropriate activities and interactions that support physical, social, emotional and cognitive growth. This study explored the relationship between active transitions in an early childhood education classroom and observable behaviour indicators of self-regulation in preschoolers, with a specific focus on the integration of yoga during transitional times. The objective was to investigate the impact of incorporating yoga on student self-regulation during large group literacy, as perceived by the preschool teacher. The research employed a collaborative action research design, engaging a preschool teacher in a reflective and systematic approach to improve classroom practices. Findings indicated that the integration of yoga, when including both challenging and sedentary poses, was associated with reductions in teacher-observed off-task behaviour during large group literacy, suggesting a possible positive influence on behaviour self-regulation. Results indicated that active transitions may support overall classroom management, increased instructional time and contributed to a comprehensive understanding of the effects of physical activity on young learners.

keyword_papers.title: Developmentally aligned AI: a framework for translating the science of child development into AI design
keyword_papers.abstract: What would it mean to design AI not for the average user, but for the child whose fingers still miss the screen, who forgets the instructions halfway through, and who greets the voice in the box as a friend? This paper proposes Developmentally Aligned Design (DAD) as a practical and ethical framework for building AI systems that meet children where they are—cognitively, socially, and emotionally. Building on the long-standing principle of developmentally appropriate practice in early childhood education, it theorises four principles of developmentally-aligned design: (1) perceptual fit (e.g., anonymised phoneme‑error tuning in early‑reading apps that respects toddlers’ speech‑production limits) (2) cognitive scaffolding (e.g. Zone‑of‑Proximal‑Development (ZPD) progressions that govern when a tutoring agent introduces harder tasks) (3) interface simplicity (e.g., storybook apps that cap menu depth and visual clutter to match preschoolers’ working‑memory span) and (4) relational integrity (e.g., conversational agents that introduce themselves with a developmentally clear disclaimer—“I’m a computer helper, not a real friend”). Through illustrative examples, it demonstrates how developmental science can serve as a validation layer on AI dataset curation, model fine‑tuning, and user experience choices. Adopting Developmentally Aligned Design can therefore sensitise AI systems to the distinct perceptual, cognitive, and socio‑emotional needs of young children; shift the responsibility of “proof of safety” from parents and early‑years practitioners to AI developers and vendors; and help the science of child development become a core intellectual engine of next‑generation AI innovation.

keyword_papers.title: The Future of Child Development in the AI Era. Cross-Disciplinary Perspectives Between AI and Child Development Experts
keyword_papers.abstract: This report explores the potential implications of rapidly integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications into children's environments. The introduction of AI in our daily lives necessitates scrutiny considering the significant role of the environment in shaping cognition, socio-emotional skills, and behaviors, especially during the first 25 years of cerebral development. As AI becomes prevalent in educational and leisure activities, it will significantly modify the experiences of children and adolescents, presenting both challenges and opportunities for their developmental trajectories. This analysis was informed by consulting with 15 experts from pertinent disciplines (AI, product development, child development, and neurosciences), along with a comprehensive review of scientific literature on children development and child-technology interactions. Overall, AI experts anticipate that AI will transform leisure activities, revolutionize education, and redefine human-machine interactions. While AI offers substantial benefits in fostering interactive engagement, it also poses risks that require careful considerations, especially during sensitive developmental periods. The report advocates for proactive international collaboration across multiple disciplines and increased research into how technological innovations affect child development. Such efforts are crucial for designing a sustainable and ethical future for the next generation through specific child-centered regulations, and helping to educate all potential stakeholders (regulators, developers, parents and educators, children) about responsible AI use and its potential impacts on child development.

keyword_papers.title: AI, Brain, and Child: navigating the intersection of artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and child development
keyword_papers.abstract: In an era marked by rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and cognitive neuroscience, the intersection of these fields holds transformative potential for child development and educational practices. This launch editorial introduces AI, Brain and Child (ABC), an open-access journal dedicated to exploring the dynamic interplay between AI, neuroscience, and child education. By fostering an interdisciplinary dialogue among educators, researchers, clinicians, and policymakers, ABC aims to examine the multifaceted roles of AI and neuroscience in shaping cognitive, social, and emotional growth among children. The journal seeks to democratize access to high-quality research, addressing both the beneficial applications and ethical challenges posed by AI and neuroscience technologies. Through this platform, ABC aspires to promote evidence-based practices, enhance educational outcomes, and tackle pressing developmental and educational issues. By welcoming diverse contributions—from empirical research to policy analysis—ABC endeavors to bridge the gaps between theory and practice, equipping stakeholders with the insights needed to navigate the complexities of educating children within a technologically enriched landscape. This new scholarly endeavor marks a new era of global community to partake in the crucial conversation surrounding the opportunities and responsibilities inherent in integrating AI and neuroscience into education.

keyword_papers.title: AI-Driven Design of Emotionally Supportive Toys for Child Development: An Iterative Process
keyword_papers.abstract: Background Emotional support is critical for children's social skills and well-being. Children exposed to emotional support at an early age can foster resilience and interpersonal skills. As traditional support methods lack interactive and personalized engagement, innovative, technology-driven solutions are consequently developed. Objective This project aimed to develop an AI-driven “emotional mentor” embodied in a plush bear whose inherent characteristic is comfort and companionship. The goal was to create a visually appealing and emotionally supportive tool that encourages children to recognize and express their feelings through gentle interaction. The design specifically targets children aged 3-11, a critical period of emotional development defined by Freudian psychology. Method The project utilized AI visual generation models guided by precise prompts, following a systematic, iterative design process. Initial design concepts were generated by AI visual generation models with precise prompts. Early outputs were critically evaluated for inconsistencies, excessive detail, and unwanted features. After iterative updates, the prompts can finally output simplicity, warmth, and an inviting appearance. LoRA fine-tuning was used to balance function and aesthetics. Market research informed the incorporation of subtle “breathing” motion effects, and user perception testing also informed the design. Results The iterative design process yielded a prototype of an emotionally supportive plush toy with refined visual aesthetics and glowing interactive features. The AI-assisted design facilitated the exploration of a range of design concepts and the systematic improvement of the toy's visual and interactive elements. Conclusion This study presents a detailed, AI-assisted iterative approach to designing an emotionally supportive plush toy. The design process and interactive visual features are the core. Future work may explore additional functionalities to further enhance the system's emotional support capabilities.

keyword_papers.title: Game-based learning in early childhood education: a systematic review and meta-analysis
keyword_papers.abstract: Game-based learning has gained popularity in recent years as a tool for enhancing learning outcomes in children. This approach uses games to teach various subjects and skills, promoting engagement, motivation, and fun. In early childhood education, game-based learning has the potential to promote cognitive, social, and emotional development. This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to summarize the existing literature on the effectiveness of game-based learning in early childhood education This systematic review and meta-analysis examine the effectiveness of game-based learning in early childhood education. The results show that game-based learning has a moderate to large effect on cognitive, social, emotional, motivation, and engagement outcomes. The findings suggest that game-based learning can be a promising tool for early childhood educators to promote children’s learning and development. However, further research is needed to address the remaining gaps in the literature. The study’s findings have implications for educators, policymakers, and game developers who aim to promote positive child development and enhance learning outcomes in early childhood education.

keyword_papers.title: Enhancing Early Childhood Mathematics Skills Learning through Digital Game-Based Learning
keyword_papers.abstract: The present study investigates the unique impact of digital game-based learning (DGBL) on children's mathematical problem-solving skills, with a particular focus on both immediate and long-term effects. While much of the existing research on DGBL explores its general benefits, this study differentiates itself by examining how DGBL specifically enhances cognitive skills. The study included 120 students, 61 of whom were assigned to an experimental group taught using digital games, and 59 to a control group taught through traditional methods. The research design incorporated the development of a customized game-based learning material and a comprehensive mathematical problem-solving assessment. The results revealed that the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group in both immediate and delayed post-tests, which underscores the effectiveness of DGBL in enhancing students' retention of mathematics well beyond the initial learning phase. This suggests that DGBL is not only effective in helping students grasp mathematical concepts in the short term but also in strengthening their ability to retain and apply these concepts over time. Moreover, the study goes further by highlighting the long-term cognitive benefits of DGBL, such as the development of critical thinking, quick decision-making, and problem-solving skills. This aspect of the study distinguishes it from other research in the field as it emphasizes not just short-term academic performance, but also lasting improvements in key cognitive abilities. Based on these findings, it is recommended that teachers integrate digital game-based learning into their teaching strategies. This integration can enhance student engagement, motivate learners, and facilitate understanding of mathematical concepts.
keyword_papers.venue: International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research

keyword_papers.title: Enhancing Early Childhood Cognitive Development via Mobile Game-Based Learning Applications: Insights and Practical Experiences
keyword_papers.abstract: Early childhood cognitive development is foundational for future academic and personal success. While traditional teaching approaches often overlook technology’s potential, gamebased learning applications offer an innovative solution to enhance cognitive abilities in young children. This study evaluates the feasibility and effectiveness of a game-based learning (GBL) application for enhancing early childhood cognitive abilities. Using Research and Development (R&D) methodology, 40 children aged 5–6 were randomly assigned to experimental and control groups for an eight-week intervention. The application was developed through systematic needs analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation. ANCOVA analysis of pre- and post-test assessments demonstrated highly significant effects (F = 2154.89, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.966), explaining 96.6% of score variations. Expert validation scores exceeded 4.6 out of 5.0, confirming the application’s quality. Qualitative feedback from teachers and parents noted substantial improvements in children’s problem-solving skills, memory retention, and critical thinking. These findings suggest that integrating GBL applications could enhance educational equity and improve cognitive development outcomes across diverse educational settings.
keyword_papers.venue: International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies

keyword_papers.title: Enhancing Early Childhood Students’ Computational Thinking Competency Through Digital Game-Based Learning
keyword_papers.abstract: This study investigated how the computational thinking competencies of students classified in the early childhood category can be developed through digital game-based learning. Computational thinking is a way of thinking that includes problem solving, algorithmic thinking and logical inference skills is considered an important competence that should be acquired at an early age. Digital game-based learning stands out as a powerful tool for developing computational thinking skills while providing a fun and motivating environment by ensuring the active participation of students. Within the scope of the research, the effects of digital game-based learning activities on students’ computational thinking skills were examined by experimental method, one of the quantitative research methods. In this study, a 4-week training activity was conducted for the experimental and control groups determined during the research process to develop computational thinking skills in 5-year-old pre-school children. The study group consists of 50 students in the 5-year-old age group studying in the pre-school class of a state institution. In the study, student groups were divided into experimental and control groups. The experimental and control groups consisted of 25 students. The achievement test prepared for the cognitive domain was used as a pre-test and post-test as the data collection tool. In addition to this data collection tool, an evaluation rubric was also used in the study. The findings showed that digital game-based learning methods positively affect the development of computational thinking skills in early childhood. In light of these findings, recommendations were made in the study for the integration of digital games into relevant educational programs and the promotion of computational thinking at an early age.
keyword_papers.venue: International Journal of Cognitive Research in Science, Engineering and Education

keyword_papers.title: Phygital Game-Based Learning in Early Childhood Education: An Exploratory Review
keyword_papers.abstract: This paper examines the role of phygital game-based learning (PGBL) in early childhood education, with a specific focus on its potential to foster critical thinking and problem-solving skills in children aged 3 to 8 years. PGBL refers to hybrid educational tools that combine physical manipulatives with interactive digital interfaces, offering multisensory and responsive learning experiences that aim to enhance cognitive engagement and symbolic reasoning. Through a literature-based qualitative review, the study analyzes five representative tools—Osmo Tangram, KIBO Robot, LEGO DUPLO Stories, Marbotic Smart Letters, and PlayShifu Orboot Earth—selected for their pedagogical relevance, documented educational use, and theoretical grounding. Drawing from constructivist and socio-cultural learning theories, particularly those of Piaget, Papert, and Vygotsky, the paper explores how these tools embody principles such as hands-on learning, scaffolding, iterative exploration, and meaningful play. Each tool is evaluated in terms of its support for higher-order cognitive functions, including sequencing, spatial reasoning, emergent literacy, and collaborative learning. The findings reveal that while PGBL tools show promise in promoting engagement and foundational executive functions, their effectiveness depends on factors such as design flexibility, ease of integration into pedagogical practice, and inclusivity. Implementation challenges such as limited open-ended play, cognitive overload, unequal access to digital infrastructure, and the need for educator training are critically examined using Universal Design for Learning (UDL) and Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) frameworks. Rather than presenting definitive causal claims, this review provides a structured synthesis of current academic literature, highlighting both the affordances and limitations of phygital tools in early education. The analysis also underscores the importance of aligning PGBL tools with developmentally appropriate practices and culturally responsive pedagogy. By offering insights across tool design, implementation, and impact, the paper aims to inform educators, researchers, and policymakers seeking to enhance early learning environments through evidence-based, interactive technologies.
keyword_papers.venue: European Conference on Games Based Learning

keyword_papers.title: EduTalkAI: Conversational Voice Assistant for Personalized Learning (for Children)
keyword_papers.abstract: The process of adaptation of personalized learning to children population is characterized by great complexity due to the age, cognitive development and engagement rates variation. Traditional e-learning environments often rely on text based content, which might not suit younger students who take more advantage of interactive, naturally communicative learning environments. In the paper, we present EduTalkAI, a conversational voice assistant designed with a particular purpose of encouraging subject-specific learning in children through interactive speech-based communication. The system includes advanced speech-recognition systems, natural-language processing, and dynamic personalization systems so as to provide context-sensitive explanations in such disciplines as mathematics, science, and language acquisition. A prototype of the EduTalkAI was tested on a group of thirty children between the ages of 7 and 12 years, showing that there was a considerable improvement in engagement, relevance of responses and acceptance of feedback as compared to baseline methodologies. This data suggests that EduTalkAI is an adaptive voice assistant that is more effective than general-purpose voice assistants, such as Google Assistant, Alexa Kids, and ChatGPT. The study is relevant to the new field of cognitive and collaborative robotics since it shows how conversational AI can be used to support personalized, engaging and effective learning experiences among young learners.

keyword_papers.title: Voice-Activated Learning Framework Using Raspberry Pi for Children’s Education
keyword_papers.abstract: Voice assistants are designed to understand and respond to spoken language, and are widely used in various applications, including education. This paper addresses the limitations of traditional text-based learning systems for young children while exploiting the familiarity and comfort that voice technology offers. The proposed voice assistant employed the Raspberry Pi model 3 B+ for the execution of natural language processing. The Raspberry Pi is utilized due to its versatility in providing a User-friendly interface. The device will be activated with the wake word “ROSE” and then function for the spelled words, math operations, multiplication tables, animal sounds, planetary and calendar information. The Children can engage with this device and will learn the uttering of words with an appropriate accent. The device performance is evaluated by calculating the success percentage based on the response from the system on the uttering of various words by the children. This device facilitates handsfree, voice-driven interactions and utilizes the capabilities of voice technology to create an innovative and secure educational platform for children.

keyword_papers.title: Artificial intelligence voice assistant implementation possibilities in interactive toy for preschool age children
keyword_papers.abstract: This paper presents some implementation possibilities of a speech recognition system for the languages Hungarian and Serbian. The system is integrated in an interactive toy for preschool age children that uses voice command. The development of this system is currently at its initial stages, but it shows some potential for application as a speech recognition system for Hungarian and Serbian. The system uses neural networks. The system is especially promising as the toy is aimed at young learners who benefit from interactive learning.

keyword_papers.title: Children's trust in and learning from voice assistants.
keyword_papers.abstract: As children increasingly interact with digital voice assistants, it is important to know whether they treat these devices as reliable information sources. Two studies investigated children's trust in and recall of statements made by a novel voice assistant and a human informant. In Study 1, children ages 4-5 (Mage = 5.05; 20 boys, 20 girls) and 7-8 (Mage = 7.98; 18 boys, 22 girls) from predominately White, upper middle-class families heard each informant respond to questions from multiple categories. With increasing age, children showed greater trust in the voice assistant for factual information and greater trust in the human for personal information about the experimenter identified as her friend. Endorsement of each informant's statements also predicted later recall. In Study 2, children ages 4-5 (Mage = 5.00; 20 boys, 20 girls) and 7-8 (Mage = 8.03; 19 boys, 21 girls) from predominately White, upper middle-class families chose whether to seek out information from a voice assistant or human informant. With increasing age, children showed an increasing preference to seek factual information from the voice assistant and an increasing preference to seek personal information from the human. Additionally, children's preferences were not related to attributions of epistemic capacities to each informant nor the presence of a voice assistant in children's homes. These results suggest that children's trust in voice assistants varies with age and depends on the type of information involved. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2022 APA, all rights reserved).

keyword_papers.title: Virtual Voice Assistant In Python (Friday)
keyword_papers.abstract: We are living the era of computers where nowadays everything can be done using computers i.e., Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, have made technology very easy that now humans can interact with machines in such a way that their task can be done only by interacting with Machines i.e., Computers. Yes, we are talking about Virtual Personal Assistants (VPAs). As of now there are many such VPAs like Alexa, Bixby, Echo, Siri, Google Assistant available on desktop, mobiles and in device also but as the technology becomes easier it becomes difficult to use for particular people such as senior citizens, blind people, also children below certain age. Also, this VPAs which are present nowadays do not provide as much facilities. To overcome this, we developed voice assistant in python on windows system which provide user to perform any task without using keyboard. Also, user can send email just by giving receiver’s email and the message user wants to send. Also, now user can book a cab just by saying where he wants to go and also book bus and train tickets. Our main aim towards developing this is to make certain things more efficient.
